skill.name: Kinds of backing: facts and figures, expert, example
skill.why: Different backing does a different job. Knowing the kind helps you judge it.
skill.how: Counts or records? Facts and figures. Someone who knows? Expert. One real case? Example.

steps.say: Bilbies need our help! Here are three pieces of backing. They're all different kinds.

show.text: Rangers counted half as many bilbies as in 2015.
Dr Lin, a bilby scientist, says so.
show.nudge: This is what one person says. Where is the count?

show.text: One bilby, Pip, lost her burrow to a fox.
show.nudge: This is one bilby, one time. Where's a count of lots?

steps.ask: Tap the count you could check.
steps.win: Yes! A ranger count is facts and figures. You could look it up and check it.

steps.say: Now look at the other two pieces.

show.text: Rangers counted half as many bilbies as in 2015.
show.nudge: That's the ranger count. Which one is a person who knows?

show.text: Dr Lin, a bilby scientist, says so.
One bilby, Pip, lost her burrow to a fox.
show.nudge: That's a bilby, not someone who studies bilbies. Try again.

steps.ask: Tap the backing from someone who knows a lot.
steps.win: Yes! Dr Lin studies bilbies, so she's an expert. Pip's story is one real case: an example.

steps.say: All three are kinds of evidence. Here's how to tell them apart.

show.text: Facts and figures can be checked;
an example is one real case.

steps.ask: Rangers counted 40 bilbies. Which kind of evidence is that?

options.text: example: one real case
options.reason: Is it one thing that happened once? It's a count of many bilbies.

options.text: facts and figures: counts or records
expert: someone who knows
options.reason: Is a person who knows a lot talking? It's a count.

steps.win: Yes! A count is facts and figures. Each kind of evidence does a different job.

steps.say: Careful! This one has a number in it. Is it facts and figures?

show.text: Mo's custard set off three smoke alarms last Tuesday.

steps.ask: What kind of backing is it?

options.text: facts and figures: counts or records
options.reason: It happened once, last Tuesday. Is it a count of lots of times?

options.text: expert: someone who knows
options.reason: Is anyone who knows a lot talking here?

options.text: example: one real case

steps.win: Yes! It's one thing, one time. A number in a story doesn't make it facts and figures.

steps.say: Backing can be strong or weak. I say fruit cups would sell well at the canteen.

options.text: Sam ate a fruit cup once and liked it.
80 of 100 kids said they'd buy one.
options.reason: Eighty kids is a big count you could check. That's strong.

options.text: The canteen's records show fruit cups sold out every day.
options.reason: Records you can check are strong. Which one is just one kid?

steps.win: Yes! One kid, one time, might be a fluke. One example on its own is weak.

steps.say: Strong backing can be checked. You can find out who said it.
steps.ask: Which expert could you check up on?

options.text: my mate's uncle, who 'knows heaps'
options.reason: Who is he? What does he know? You can't check.

options.text: a man online who says he's an expert
options.reason: Anyone can say that online. Can you find out who he is?

options.text: Dr Lin, a bilby scientist at Bluster Zoo

steps.win: Yes! You can look up Dr Lin and her job. Backing you can check is stronger.

terms.means: Counts, measures or records about many cases. You can check them.
Someone who knows a lot about the topic, like a scientist.
One real case: one thing that happened, one time.

examples.text: Rangers counted half as many bilbies as in 2015.
Dr Lin, a bilby scientist, says they need help.
One bilby, Pip, lost her burrow to a fox.

card.test: A count, someone who knows, or one case? Then ask: can I check it? Is it enough?

weDo.text: Claim: Our school needs shade sails over the playground. Backing: Dr Patel, a skin doctor, says children need shade when they play outside.
weDo.prompt: What kind of backing is this?
weDo.hint: Who is talking? Do they know a lot about skin?
weDo.success: Dr Patel is a skin doctor, so she knows a lot about sun and skin. That's an expert.

options.text: facts and figures: counts or records
options.reason: There are no counts or records here. It's what one person says.

options.text: expert: someone who knows
example: one real case
options.reason: Nothing happened to one person here. Think about Dr Patel's job.

weDo.prompt: Gus claims Mo's cooking is dangerous. Match each piece of backing to its kind.
weDo.hint: Numbers? A person who knows? Or one thing that happened?
weDo.success: A count of smoke alarms is facts and figures. A chef is an expert. The spoon is one real case.

items.text: Gus tested ten of Mo's dishes, and seven set off the smoke alarm.
items.reason: Gus counted results from ten dishes. A count you could check is facts and figures.

items.text: Chef Rosa runs the hotel kitchen, and she says Mo's stove is a fire risk.
items.reason: Chef Rosa runs a big kitchen. She knows a lot about cooking safely.

items.text: Mo's fish-finger custard once melted a spoon.
items.reason: This is one thing that happened, one time. That's an example.

write.ask: Back up 'Our school needs more shade' with an expert. Combine the three facts into one sentence.
given: Ms Ruiz is the school nurse.
She has worked here for 20 years.
She treats sunburnt kids every week.
write.starter: Our school needs more shade, because
checks: I said who Ms Ruiz is.
I said how she knows so much.
I said what she sees every week.
write.model: Our school needs more shade, because Ms Ruiz, our school nurse for 20 years, treats sunburnt kids every week.

creature.name: Kindalah
creature.blurb: A galah with three crest feathers: one for facts and figures, one for experts and one for examples. Each feather pops up when it hears its kind of backing.

encounters.frame: Wren has made a poster for Bilby Day. The Kindalah is perched on top of it.
encounters.text: SAVE OUR BILBIES! Bilbies need our help. Every year, rangers count the bilbies in our park. Rangers found only half as many bilbies this year as in 2014. Bilby scientist Dr Lin says foxes and cats are their biggest danger. A fox chased a young bilby called Pip from her burrow. Wren found her and took her to the vet. Come to the Bilby Day stall on Saturday. All money goes to the Red Dust Bilby Rescue.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence from Wren's poster uses an expert?
encounters.success: Dr Lin is a bilby scientist. She knows a lot about bilbies, so she's an expert.

options.text: Rangers found only half as many bilbies this year as in 2014.
options.reason: This is a count you could check. That's facts and figures.

options.text: Bilby scientist Dr Lin says foxes and cats are their biggest danger.
A fox chased a young bilby called Pip from her burrow.
options.reason: This tells you about one bilby, one time. That's an example.

encounters.text: BRING BACK FRUIT CUPS! The canteen should sell fruit cups again. We asked 100 kids, and 80 said they would buy them. Ms Diaz is our school nurse. She says fruit gives kids energy for the afternoon. Sam had no fruit at lunch last week. He fell asleep in maths. Fruit cups only cost $2. Please sign our petition at the canteen door.
encounters.prompt: Match each piece of backing to its kind.
encounters.success: A count of 100 kids is facts and figures. The nurse knows health. Sam is one real case.

items.text: We asked 100 kids, and 80 said they would buy fruit cups.

items.text: Ms Diaz, the school nurse, says fruit gives kids energy.

items.text: Sam had no fruit at lunch and fell asleep in maths.
items.reason: This is about one kid on one day. That's an example.

encounters.frame: A letter in the Bluster Rock Bugle. The Kindalah is reading it on the beach.
encounters.prompt: Ada claims rubbish is hurting sea animals. Tap the facts and figures.

parts.reason: This is about one turtle, one time. That's an example.

parts.reason: Dr Hale knows a lot about the ocean. She's an expert.

encounters.frame: Letters about the school band keep arriving at the Bugle. The Kindalah is sorting them by feather.
encounters.text: Last week, the Bugle asked readers whether the council should give more money to the Bluster Rock Primary school band. The band practises in an old shed with a leaking roof, and many of its instruments are older than the teachers. Readers sent in lots of backing for their claims. One said the band brought 500 people to its last concert. Another sent us a long letter from a music teacher. A third told us how the band changed one shy student's life. Some readers wrote in to say the money should go to the footy club instead. The council will vote on the money next month.
encounters.prompt: Match each piece of backing to its kind.
encounters.success: Counts are facts and figures. People who know music are experts. One student's story is an example.

items.text: The band sold 500 tickets for its last concert.
items.reason: 500 tickets sold is a count you could check. That's facts and figures.

items.text: Music teacher Mr Adeyemi says every child should learn an instrument.
items.reason: A music teacher knows the topic well. He is an expert.

items.text: Lily was too shy to talk in class, but after two years in the band, she sings solos.
items.reason: Two years is a number, but it's one student's story. One real case is an example.

items.text: Nine out of ten band members say they enjoy school more since joining.
items.reason: This counts the answers of many band members. That is facts and figures.

items.text: According to Professor Grace Obi, who studies how children learn, music helps with maths.
items.reason: A professor who studies learning knows a lot about this topic. She is an expert.

encounters.frame: Indi is writing a speech about the school art room. The Kindalah is watching her draft.
encounters.text: Indi wants Bluster Rock Primary to turn the old storeroom into an art room. At the moment, students paint at their desks, and there is nowhere to dry their work. Indi has written three sentences to back up her claim. She wants one of each kind of backing: facts and figures, an expert and an example. Indi has already drawn a plan of the new room. It has easels by the windows, a long sink and a drying rack along the back wall. Mr Pettigrew, the caretaker, says the storeroom is mostly full of broken chairs and one very old cricket bat. She has asked the Kindalah to check them. The Kindalah has already eaten one of her pencils, but it is still very good at checking.
encounters.prompt: Which of Indi's sentences is an example?
encounters.success: Indi's galah is one piece of art, squashed one time. One real case is an example.

options.text: My papier-mâché galah was squashed flat under a pile of maths books.
The Year 6s counted 140 damaged paintings in the classrooms last year.
options.reason: A count with a number is facts and figures. You could check the Year 6s' tally.

options.text: Ms Rao, who trains art teachers at the university, says every school needs a place to make a mess.
options.reason: Ms Rao knows a lot about teaching art. She's an expert, not an example.

parts.tap: A blue-tongue lizard called Bluey lost the tip of her tail to a robot mower on Dune Street.

encounters.frame: Mo is trying to win the Bluster Rock Joke Cup. The Kindalah is listening, politely.
encounters.text: The Joke Cup is held every year in the Bluster Rock town hall, and the winner gets a golden rubber chicken. Mo wants the judges of the Bluster Rock Joke Cup to know that he is the funniest kid on the island. His speech to the judges is short. 'I am the funniest kid on Bluster Rock,' he says. 'For my last ten shows, I kept a tally of every laugh. Out of 400 jokes, the audience laughed at 310. I counted.' Then he bows. Then he bows again. One judge writes something down. Another judge is still trying to work out the joke about the cow.
encounters.prompt: Mo says audiences laughed at 310 of his 400 jokes. What kind of backing is this?
encounters.success: Mo kept a tally of laughs over ten shows. A count like that is facts and figures.

options.text: facts and figures: counts or records
expert: someone who knows
options.reason: Mo isn't quoting anyone who knows about comedy. Look at what he kept a tally of.

options.text: example: one real case
options.reason: He isn't telling the story of one joke or one show. He's counting results from ten shows.

encounters.frame: The Bugle is reporting on the old mine. The Kindalah is reading it with one eye shut.
encounters.prompt: The report claims the old mine is unsafe. Tap the facts and figures.
encounters.success: Two collapses out of six tunnels comes from an inspection you could check. That's facts and figures.

parts: IS THE OLD MINE SAFE? The old mine at the back of Bluster Rock closed in 1923, but ghost tours still visit it every weekend. Now some locals are saying it isn't safe.

parts.tap: Mr Karl Brandt, a mining engineer, says nobody should go past the first tunnel without a hard hat.
parts.reason: Mr Brandt knows a lot about mines. That makes him an expert.

parts.tap: A rock fell from the roof and crushed a tourist's torch on Saturday night's tour.
parts.reason: This is one thing that happened, one time. That's an example.

parts.tap: The council's inspection found that two of the mine's six tunnels have collapsed.

parts: Ghost tour guide Slick Vinnie says the mine is 'perfectly safe for brave people'. The council will decide next week whether to close it.

encounters.frame: Coach Dev Marsh has written to the Bugle about the oval. The Kindalah is checking every sentence.
encounters.text: Dear Editor, I coach the Bluster Rock Roos, our town's junior footy team. I am asking the council to put lights on the oval at Red Dune Park. In winter, the sun sets before 5:30 pm. By the time our players get to training, there is barely an hour of daylight left. Our club has more than sixty players, aged from eight to twelve. Here is my backing. Four games were called off last season because it was too dark to see the ball. Ruby Tan coaches the state's under-12 squad, and she says young players get hurt more often in poor light. On one dark night in June, three of our players tripped over the same cone. The league's injury lists tell the same story: clubs that train under lights have fewer injuries than we do. Parents have offered to run a sausage sizzle at every home game to help pay for the lights. I hope the council will listen. Yours sincerely, Dev Marsh
encounters.prompt: Which sentence from Dev's letter is an example?
encounters.success: Three players tripping on one night is one real case. A number doesn't turn one night into facts and figures.

options.text: Four games were called off last season because it was too dark to see the ball.
options.reason: This counts games across a whole season. That's facts and figures, not one case.

options.text: Ruby Tan coaches the state's under-12 squad, and she says young players get hurt more often in poor light.
options.reason: There's no title, but coaching the state's young players means she knows a lot. She's an expert.

options.text: On one dark night in June, three of our players tripped over the same cone.
The league's injury lists tell the same story: clubs that train under lights have fewer injuries than we do.
options.reason: There's no digit, but this compares injury lists across the league. That's facts and figures.

encounters.frame: Year 6 is debating sugary drinks at the canteen. The Kindalah is sorting their backing.
encounters.text: On Thursday, Year 6 debated whether the canteen should stop selling sugary drinks. Here is the backing the ban team used.
encounters.prompt: Match each piece of backing to its kind.
encounters.success: Counts are facts and figures, digits or not. Experts know a lot. One case is an example, number or not.

items.reason: It starts with 'Last term', but it counts a whole term's sales. That's facts and figures.

items.text: Rosa cleans children's teeth at the town clinic, and she says sugary drinks cause most of the holes she sees.
items.reason: There's no title, but cleaning children's teeth every day means she knows a lot. She's an expert.

items.text: Ruby's dentist found three holes in her teeth after a term of daily soft drinks.
items.reason: A dentist and a number are in it, but it's one girl's teeth. One real case is an example.

items.text: Every class that swapped to water this year had fewer visits to the sick bay.
items.reason: There's no digit, but this counts sick bay visits for every class. That's facts and figures.

items.text: Coach Dunn trains the state's junior runners and says water is the best drink for sport.
items.reason: Coach Dunn trains top young athletes, so she knows a lot about sport. She is an expert.

items.text: Leo stopped getting headaches once he swapped soft drinks for water.
items.reason: This tells about one boy. A single story is an example, even if it is convincing.

items.text: Seventy of the 120 students asked said they feel tired after sugary drinks.
items.reason: This counts many students' answers. That's facts and figures.

encounters.frame: Wren has written to the council about the library. The Kindalah has its expert feather up.
encounters.prompt: Wren claims the library needs a giant beanbag. Tap the expert.

Zed is a little nervous, because the last time he spoke at assembly, his microphone stopped working halfway through. This time, he has practised in front of the mirror, the crew and the Kindalah, which fell asleep.

encounters.frame: Maxx is backing up his claim about the Moon trip. The Kindalah is suspicious, but it's still sorting.
encounters.text: Maxx it out, Vantafam! Some of you haters are still saying my trip to the Moon is impossible. Well, I've got backing, and lots of it. My team has collected numbers, quotes from experts and real stories, so get ready to be proven wrong. I've put my four best sentences below. Read them, and then tell all your friends that Maxx Vantablack was right all along. The Gold Rocket is thirty metres tall, it has four seats, and yes, the waterslide is real. I've been training for months, mostly by spinning round and round in my office chair until I feel sick. My hair stylist is coming too, because zero gravity is very bad for volume. The launch will be streamed in gold-tinted high definition. Two Xs, because one X is for losers! Remember, the launch is on 3 March, and tickets to watch it from the beach are still on sale at the Vantamart for just $50. Smash that heart button like it owes you money! Stay gold!
encounters.prompt: Which of Maxx's sentences uses facts and figures?
encounters.success: 'Every test flight' counts many flights, even with no digits. Darren's trip is one case, even with a number.

options.text: Nova Starr has built more rockets than anyone in the country, and she says mine is ready for space.
options.reason: There's no title, but she has built more rockets than anyone. She knows a lot: an expert.

options.text: My cousin Darren and two mates rode the Gold Rocket and came back without a scratch.
options.reason: There's a number, but it's one trip, one time. That makes it an example.

options.text: The Gold Rocket has landed safely on every one of its test flights so far.
Everyone knows the trip is possible, because I am Maxx Vantablack and I always win.
options.reason: This isn't backing at all. It just asks you to trust Maxx because he's Maxx.

encounters.frame: A newspaper story about a new crossing near the school. The Kindalah is waiting at the kerb.
encounters.prompt: The article claims the school needs a crossing. Tap the example.

parts: PARENTS CALL FOR SCHOOL CROSSING. Parents at Bluster Rock Primary are asking the council to build a pedestrian crossing on Dune Street, outside the school's main gate. The street is busy in the mornings, with utes, road trains and tourist buses all passing through.

parts.tap: A traffic count last month found that more than 400 vehicles use Dune Street between 8 am and 9 am.
parts.reason: A traffic count gives numbers you could check. That's facts and figures.

parts.tap: Lee Moana has taught road safety in hundreds of schools, and she says a crossing would make the street much safer.
parts.reason: There's no title, but teaching road safety in hundreds of schools means she knows a lot. She's an expert.

parts.tap: A ute missed Year 3 student Ella Vance by less than one metre on Monday.
Every school on the highway that got a crossing has had fewer near misses since.
parts.reason: There's no digit, but this compares every school on the highway. That's facts and figures.

parts: Several parents have offered to help paint the crossing lines if the council agrees. The council says it will look at the request at its next meeting. In the meantime, Principal Okafor has asked parents to drop their children at the back gate, where the road is quieter.

encounters.frame: Ada Pennick's letter about jet skis is going to the council. The Kindalah has all three feathers up.
encounters.text: Dear Councillors, I am writing on behalf of the Bluster Bay Turtle Volunteers to ask you to cancel the licence that allows jet ski hire in the bay. For decades, the northern end of the bay has been a nesting beach for green turtles. Since the hire shop opened in October, our work has changed. I have gathered four pieces of backing for my claim that jet skis are hurting the turtles. First, the rangers found fourteen injured turtles this summer, compared with two last summer. Second, marine biologist Dr Iris Ferris, who tracks the bay's turtles by satellite, warns that engine noise drives nesting females away. Third, one turtle, which we named Shelly, had a propeller cut so deep that she needed six weeks of care. Fourth, a post on a fishing forum, signed only 'TurtleGuy', says he has worked with turtles for years and that jet skis scare them. My nephew says one of these is much weaker than the others. I would be grateful if you could read them before the vote on 12 December. Yours faithfully, Ada Pennick, turtle volunteer
encounters.prompt: Ada's nephew says one piece of backing is much weaker than the others. Which one, and why?
encounters.success: Backing you can't check is weak. You can look up Dr Ferris and the rangers, but not a forum name.

options.text: TurtleGuy: he claims years with turtles, but nobody can check who he is.
Shelly: one turtle could be a fluke, so her story is the weakest piece.
options.reason: One case is weaker than a count, but Shelly's cut is real, and the rangers could confirm it.

options.text: The rangers' count: a single summer of numbers could easily be a fluke.
options.reason: Fourteen against two is a big jump, and you could check the rangers' count.

options.text: Dr Ferris: she studies turtles, not jet skis, so it's outside her field.
options.reason: Her warning is about what engine noise does to turtles. That's her field, and you could look her up.

encounters.frame: The Bugle has printed an opinion piece about the music festival. The Kindalah is sorting it, feather by feather.
encounters.text: Jojo Reyes plays in the band Red Dust Static, and she wants the council to bring back the Bluster Rock Music Festival. Her opinion piece in the Bugle gives the seven pieces of backing below.
encounters.prompt: Match each piece of Jojo's backing to its kind. Some are tricky.
encounters.success: Facts and figures count, even in words. Experts know a field. One case is an example, however big its numbers.

items.text: About 6,000 visitors came to the 2019 festival, the council's report says.
items.reason: A council report with visitor numbers can be checked. That's facts and figures.

items.text: Every shop on the main street took more money that weekend than on any other weekend of 2019.
items.reason: There's no digit, but this compares every shop's takings. That's facts and figures.

items.text: Rosa Ferri, who has run the shopkeepers' group through twelve festivals, says they bring customers to every shop.
items.reason: Twelve is a number, but it is about what Rosa knows. Leading the shopkeepers makes her an expert.

items.text: Tourism researcher Professor Lena Watts says country festivals bring visitors back year after year.
items.reason: A professor who researches tourism knows the topic well. She is an expert.

items.text: Local singer Tash Moore played to 6,000 people that year and was offered her first recording contract.
items.reason: Big numbers, but it's what happened to one singer. A single story is an example.

items.text: The Nguyen family drove 900 kilometres to the festival and stayed at the caravan park for a week.
items.reason: 900 kilometres is a number, but it's one family's trip. That's an example.

items.text: Two in every three residents who were asked would like the festival to return.
items.reason: This counts many people's answers, even written in words. That's facts and figures.

encounters.frame: A report in the Bugle asks whether Maxx's auction money reached the Rescue Fund. The Kindalah is reading it very closely.
encounters.prompt: The editor wants to cut the weakest piece of backing for the report's claim. Tap it.
encounters.success: Kai knows surfing, not charities. Being famous doesn't make him an expert, so his word adds little.

parts: WHERE DID THE MONEY GO? Last month, Maxx Vantablack auctioned his painting 'Gold on Gold' and promised that every cent would go to the Maxx Vantablack Rescue Fund. The Bugle has been trying to find out what the fund actually spends its money on. So far, the answers have raised more questions than they have settled.

parts.tap: The fund's own published accounts show that only $3,000 of the $90,000 it raised last year was spent on animal care.
parts.reason: Published accounts with figures can be checked. That is strong backing.

parts.tap: Accountant Harriet Cole, whose job is checking charities' books, says a fund spending so little should be investigated.
parts.reason: Checking charities is her job, and you could look her up. That is strong.

parts.tap: The fund promised to pay for an injured koala's operation, but the money never arrived, and volunteers paid instead.
parts.reason: It's one case, but the volunteers could confirm it. That's real backing.

parts.tap: Champion surfer Kai Brooks told his two million fans online that the fund is 'a total scam'.

parts: The Bugle has asked to see the fund's receipts for the past three years. We will report what we find. Readers who have donated to the fund are encouraged to ask for receipts too. A spokesperson for Maxx said the fund was 'doing amazing things'.

encounters.frame: Gus's robotics club proposal has a judging problem. The Kindalah found it straight away.
encounters.text: Gus has five minutes at the school council meeting to argue for a robotics club at Bluster Rock Primary. He has three pieces of backing, one of each kind. First, he has a quote from Professor Dana Liu, who designs robots for hospitals and believes every primary school should teach children to build simple machines. Second, he has a national study, which found that schools with robotics clubs had a 20 per cent rise in students choosing science in high school. Third, he has the story of Saltbush Creek Primary, whose Year 6 robotics team built a robot that waters the school garden and won a state prize. Indi wrote a note on the poster beside each piece, saying how strong it is. She was drawing a robot in the margin at the time, and one note is wrong. Gus has rehearsed his speech eleven times, mostly in front of Mo, who now says the words along with him. He is also bringing his own robot, Sorty, to show the council what students can build.
encounters.prompt: Tap Indi's wrong note. Then choose a better one.
encounters.success: One school's prize is real, but it can't show every school would do as well. It might be a fluke.

parts.reason: That's right. Results from many schools are hard to fluke.

parts.reason: That's right. You can check who she is and what she does.

weak, because examples are never really true

encounters.frame: The collar company has sent the Vantamart buyers a second pitch. The Kindalah is comparing them, nose held.
encounters.text: The collar company first sent the buyers one story: 'The Patel family's dog, Rufus, wore our stink-proof collar for a month and never once needed a bath.' Now it has sent a second pitch: 'Twenty dogs wore our collar for a month, and not one of them needed a bath.'
encounters.prompt: What kind of backing is the second pitch, and how does it compare with Rufus's story?
encounters.success: Twenty dogs is a count you could check. One dog might be a fluke, but twenty is far harder.

options.text: Facts and figures: it counts twenty dogs, so it's less likely to be a fluke.
Example: twenty dogs in one test is still just one story, like Rufus.
options.reason: One story is about one dog. Counting twenty dogs' results is a check anyone could repeat.

options.text: Expert: the company tested twenty dogs, so it knows its collar best.
options.reason: Nobody who knows a lot is speaking here. It's a count of dogs.

options.text: Facts and figures: but it's weaker, because more dogs means more chances to go wrong.
options.reason: More dogs makes a fluke less likely, not more. Twenty results beat one.

encounters.frame: The Bugle has a follow-up story on the mystery lights. The Kindalah is reading it under the doona.
encounters.prompt: The report claims the lights are probably not ghosts. Tap the expert on this topic.
encounters.success: Esther Okafor studies glowing fungi, so she knows this topic. Dr Mehta knows teeth, and his is one sighting.

parts: MYSTERY LIGHTS: NOT GHOSTS AFTER ALL? For two weeks now, strange green lights have been appearing above the old mine at the back of Bluster Rock, and ghost tour guide Slick Vinnie has been telling visitors that they are the spirits of long-gone miners. Ticket sales for his midnight tour have tripled. But the Bugle has found growing reasons to think that the lights have a far more ordinary explanation.

parts.tap: The council took readings on five nights, and the lights appeared only when the air was warm and damp.
parts.reason: Readings over five nights are measured records. That's facts and figures.

parts.tap: Dr Raj Mehta, a dentist, says he watched the lights glow and fade from his kitchen window on Friday.
parts.reason: He has a 'Dr', but he knows teeth, not lights. His sighting is one real case: an example.

parts.tap: Esther Okafor studies glowing fungi, and she says the colour matches one that grows on old mine timbers.
A local teenager, Kade, crept into the mine's entrance on Thursday and photographed a glowing patch on a wooden beam.
parts.reason: Kade's photo is one real case, from one night. That makes it an example.

parts: Slick Vinnie has not commented, although a box of green glow sticks was seen in the back of his ute on Tuesday. The Soggy Biscuit crew has offered to help the council investigate, and their engineer, Gus, has asked to take a small sample of the fungus home for testing. Mo has asked whether it can be eaten.
